As of 245 AM EDT...

KEY MESSAGE 1... 

Zonal flow aloft and sfc high pressure centered in eastern
Quebec will continue our stretch of beautiful weather today
across eastern NY and western New England. Expect plenty of 
sunshine mixed diurnally driven cumulus, comfortable humidity, 
and temperatures warming into the low to mid 80s in the valley 
with mid to upper 70s in the higher terrain. Skies clear this
evening allowing temperatures to cool but overnight temperatures
likely will not be quite as cool as previous nights given
increasing clouds tracking west to east into the region. Coolest
temperatures should occur in western New England where skies
will stay clear longest supporting radiational cooling and
overnight lows falling comfortably into the low to mid 50s. High
pressure starts to move further to our east tomorrow into the
Canadian Maritimes with broad troughing from the Great Lakes
building into the Northeast. Weak subsidence from high pressure
to our northeast looks to maintain enough subsidence to keep
most areas dry except the southwest Adirondacks and northern 
and eastern Catskills where broad troughing and weak height 
falls along with additional lift from the terrain can support 
isolated to scattered showers or thunderstorms. However, given
very low shear and low instability, severe weather is not
expected. Our western areas are only outlined in SPC's general
thunder. 

KEY MESSAGE 2...

Cloud coverage and humidity increases heading into Monday as
broad troughing remains overhead and wind aloft becoming west-
southwesterly. While height falls are minimal, temperatures
aloft cool supporting mid-level lapse rates around 5.5 - 6C/km
which when combined with breaks of sun and dew points rising
into the 60s will likely contribute to increased sfc based
instability reaching 500 - 1000 J/kg. Very weak flow aloft once
again will keep shear negligible so as isolated to scattered 
diurnally driven showers/storms develop, they will likely be 
slow moving and quickly dissipate. Higher terrain areas 
including the southwest Adirondacks and eastern Catskills are 
most favored for any isolated to scattered shower/storm. SPC 
maintain just general thunder across eastern NY and western New 
England.

There is increasing confidence that we will enter into a more
unsettled period Tuesday into Wednesday with widespread likely
and even categorical POPs both days across eastern NY and
western New England. This is attributed to a stronger shortwave
rounding the top of the expansive ridge positioned across the 
Central and Western CONUS and amplifying as it digs into the 
Great Lakes and Northeast. While there is medium to high
confidence that the middle of the week will include showers and
thunderstorms, there remains uncertainty on the timing and
amplitude of this shortwave which will be important as we 
diagnosis which hazards will be at play. There are two main
scenarios with the first suggesting the shortwave closes off
over the Great Lakes or Ohio Valley, supporting strong southerly
flow ahead of it that advects a strong plume of Gulf moisture
into the Northeast Tues into Wed. This would increase the
chances for heavy downpours from thunderstorms and potential for
heavy rain to repeatedly impact a given area increasing the
chance for isolated instances of flooding. The second solution
suggests a delay in the shortwave amplifying until it is further
east. Increased upper level divergence ahead of it interacts
with a stalled boundary that has been impacting the
Carolinas/mid-Atlantic for the past few days resulting in a
coastal low developing and tracking to southern New England. We
would likely be positioned within the cool conveyor belt north
of the boundary and sfc low leading to more widespread stratiform
rain. The latest NBM still shows 30 to 60% chance for at least
1" of rain across eastern NY and western New England between 8PM
Tues and 8PM Wed with a 15 to 35% for over 2 inches. As was 
mentioned in the previous discussion, dry antecedent conditions 
heading into this event keep flooding concerns low as high 
flash flood guidance values indicate soils should be able to 
handle 1 to 2 inches of rain falling over multiple hours. If the
first scenario ends up occurring, flooding concerns will likely
increase as this favors convection potentially repeatedly 
impacting a given area. Latest WPC Excessive Rainfall Outlook 
shows widespread Marginal Risk both Tues and Wed suggesting 
isolated instances for flash flooding potential. This product 
will update again tonight.
